answerEvidence.summary: A dedicated stored policy binds the intended group of service SAS grants to shared server-side constraints that can be revoked without rotating the signing account key.

answerEvidence.summary: The mixed secured/regular-hub example explicitly states that the internet default route does not propagate across hubs, so inter-hub connectivity alone cannot supply East egress to West.

The guide distinguishes Private-policy traffic from internet egress and retains the cross-hub default-route restriction; adding a Private policy in East does not create that propagation.

answerEvidence.summary: The gateway prerequisites prohibit Basic and policy-based configurations, the tunnel/authentication instructions specify OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID, and the address-pool section requires a private range disjoint from the destination VNet and connecting on-premises location. A compatible non-Basic route-based gateway with that tunnel and pool is the only offered revision that removes all the proposed incompatibilities. It does not replace the remaining tenant and client-profile setup steps.

distractorEvidence.summary: Retaining the proposed Basic policy-based gateway violates both explicit Entra P2S gateway restrictions, and SSTP is not the required OpenVPN tunnel type. Registering an older audience cannot repair either network prerequisite. Older manually registered audiences are not claimed to be already unsupported: the receipt allows them on compatible Windows clients until the future retirement dates.

The client-pool instructions require private addresses that do not overlap the destination VNet or the on-premises connection origin. Keeping the stated overlapping pool violates that condition regardless of the authentication label. It also leaves the proposed incompatible gateway unchanged, so this is not a complete revision.

Even if compatible gateway here means choosing a supported SKU, the retained policy-based type is expressly excluded for Entra P2S, and the retained overlap violates the separate address-pool requirement. If compatible instead means the whole gateway, the option contradicts its own retained policy-based setting. Neither reading resolves the listed defects.

answerEvidence.summary: For an automation rule created while signed into the provider tenant and a customer-tenant playbook, the multitenant section explicitly instructs the provider to find Azure Security Insights under Enterprise applications filtered to Microsoft Applications, copy its Object ID, and use that value as principalId in an extra Lighthouse authorization. Its example supplies exactly the question role GUID f4c81013-99ee-4d62-a7ee-b3f1f648599a; the roles article confirms this authorizes Sentinel rather than a human operator.

distractorEvidence.summary: The MSSP procedure requires an extra Lighthouse authorization for the provider tenant Azure Security Insights application after customer permissions are set. The roles article identifies Automation Contributor as a service permission, not a user-account role. Reusing the already-delegated human operator Object ID would still omit the service application required by this automation path.

The provider-side steps direct the administrator to copy the Object ID of the Azure Security Insights enterprise application into principalId. A customer directory tenant ID identifies the tenant, not the provider service application whose extra authorization is missing; the existing customer-side playbook grant does not change the required principal field.

The documented authorization entry requires the provider Azure Security Insights application Object ID as principalId, whereas the playbook is the separate Logic Apps resource to which execution access is needed. Supplying the customer workflow Azure resource ID identifies the target resource instead of the service principal and cannot fill the documented extra-authorization field.

rubric.notes: Alignment (2): the current Sentinel automation/playbooks subskill includes implementing the cross-tenant permission path, not merely recognizing a product name. Accuracy (2): the provider Azure Security Insights Object ID, Microsoft Applications filter, both-tenant authorization and fixed role GUID all appear in the actual multitenant implementation section. Scenario completeness (2): customer playbook location, provider sign-in, satisfied customer grant and already-delegated human isolate the remaining principal without implying that the snippet alone performs onboarding. Distractor plausibility (1): human identity versus service identity is a relevant confusion; a directory ID and a workflow resource ID are easier category errors, and a customer-side service-principal Object ID would be a stronger alternative. Answer uniqueness (2): only b identifies the documented provider enterprise application; the other IDs identify a human, tenant or resource, regardless of their existing access. Documentation strength (2): the direct run-playbooks procedure provides the exact field, GUID and surrounding prerequisites, and the independent roles source supports the service-account distinction; official supplemental lifecycle evidence names the GA automation features. Difficulty authenticity (1): provider/customer authorization is specialized enough for lower-end advanced exposure, but the explicit missing-service-app clue and single principalId blank require less reasoning than a strong advanced engineering problem; this is not expert or substantial code-debugging depth. Explanation quality (2): the explanation identifies the correct tenant and lookup path, and separately rejects each wrong identity category without equating human delegation with service execution. Originality (2): sc200-002 tests the service role on the playbook resource group, already given here; this replacement tests the distinct provider Lighthouse application-Object-ID step. sc500-129 human authoring roles and sc500-140 trigger matching also test different contracts.
